page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: It cannot give constants
lines: Dimensional analysis cannot find the value of a
pure number in a formula, because a number
The 2π in T = 2π√(l/g) is an example.
steps.why: The method compares powers of M, L and T. A pure number contributes nothing to any of those powers, so it leaves no trace to recover.
common_mistakes: Saying it cannot be used at all for such formulas. It gives every power correctly; only the number is missing.

recall.must_convey: That it cannot give the value of a dimensionless constant such as two pi.

steps.memory_tip: It finds the powers, never the number in front.
steps.margin_note: Give the 2π example. It makes the limitation concrete.

steps.label: The other limits

lines.text: It fails for sums, and for more than three unknowns

lines: An equation with added terms such as
s = ut + ½at² cannot be derived this way.
steps.why: The method assumes a single product of powers. A sum of two terms is not of that form, so there is nothing for the method to match.
common_mistakes: Saying it cannot check s = ut + ½at². It can check that equation; it cannot derive it.

recall.must_convey: That it cannot derive equations with added terms, cannot handle more than three unknowns, and cannot handle trigonometric or exponential functions.

steps.memory_tip: The method builds ONE product of powers, so a sum defeats it.
steps.margin_note: Derive versus check is the distinction to keep.

insider_note: Four limitations are listed here (constant; sums; more than three unknowns; trigonometric, exponential or logarithmic functions); two written clearly is enough for two marks. Lead with the constant.
